overview: Tekohá (Guarani) is the atlas label, but its 1492 polygon is not one state, border, language area, or timeless Guarani society. Guarani sources describe tekoha as a place where a way of life is made through families, land, forest, water, gardens, medicines, relationships, and spiritual practice. That meaning cannot be stretched from eastern Bolivia and Paraguay to Rio de Janeiro and Porto Alegre simply because one map color does. Mbyá, Kaiowa or Paĩ Tavyterã, and Ñandeva or Avá Guarani communities have related yet distinct speech, histories, customs, and political life. Archaeology adds another caution: pottery styles, dark earth, house traces, crops, fish bones, and village plans reveal regional practices, but artifacts do not automatically name their makers. This card therefore uses dated local evidence to explore settlements, farming, fishing, hunting, pottery, family work, children’s learning, health, water, and waste around 1492. It marks later ethnography as comparison, not a frozen survival. No securely localized Guarani writing from 1492 to 1500 is known. The feature’s disappearance in 1500 records an atlas repaint, not the end of any people or tekoha.

periods.title: One polygon cannot be one tekoha
periods.summary: The 1492 layer introduces a single vast Tekohá (Guarani) feature. Guarani explanations make tekoha specific to community relationships and lived places, while the polygon crosses many environments and peoples. The first lesson is therefore cartographic correction, not an invented eight-year state.

periods.title: The map overlaps distinct names
periods.summary: At several tested coordinates the target overlaps Mbyá, Charrua, Puri, Kaiowa, Ñandeva, or other labels. Three direct arc neighbors are only TopoJSON seams. Neither stacking nor shared arcs demonstrates a shared government, language, ancestry, alliance, or everyday territorial administration or identity.

periods.title: Regional dates replace blanket ancestry
periods.summary: Site chronologies show Guarani-associated materials across the Paraná basin and southern coast before European invasion, but distributions and dates vary. Archaeologists model movement through rivers, forests, and coasts while debating connections. A dated ceramic context is stronger evidence than an atlas-wide origin story.

periods.title: Iguazú preserves multiple histories
periods.summary: Systematic work around Iguazú Falls found both lithic-only contexts and places with Guarani pottery, plus radiocarbon dates. Even one famous landscape holds different occupations. Investigators must separate layers and material traditions before deciding which activities belong together or which name may fit.

periods.title: Houses and black earth need context
periods.summary: São Paulo ethnoarchaeology compares dark anthropogenic soils with large-house locations and settlement patterns. The approach can explain how traces form, but analogy is not time travel. Each soil patch still needs excavation, dating, and regional comparison before becoming a family, village, or named people.

periods.title: Pots preserve meals and choices
periods.summary: Misiones vessels preserve maize and squash microremains and forms associated with cooking, storage, serving, and drinking. Those traces illuminate particular collections, not every household. Vessel names drawn from later sources remain interpretive tools, and a painted sherd cannot announce its maker’s identity.

periods.title: The southern edge stays complicated
periods.summary: Evidence in Uruguay and the lower Paraná is sparse, uneven, and sometimes poorly contextualized. Recent projects improve dates and residential evidence, but the southern boundary remains a research question. The atlas line should not turn scattered finds into a surveyed frontier or uniform population.

periods.title: The endpoint is an atlas repaint
periods.summary: At 1500 the exact id disappears, while representative points receive broad or different labels that remain stable in 1530. No source documents a synchronized Guarani collapse, migration, conquest, or language shift in that instant. The transition belongs to the files, not to human continuity.

sections.title: Correct the atlas before using the label

items.text: The exact record appears once, only in world-1492.json, as one polygon with one ring and 148 decoded positions. Its bounds run from about 65.16 degrees west to 40.19 west and 33.05 degrees south to 14.26 south. These are drawing measurements, not surveyed borders.

Asunción, Ciudad del Este, Encarnación, Santa Cruz, Campo Grande, Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo, Curitiba, Porto Alegre, Posadas, and Rivera test inside. Brasília, Belo Horizonte, Florianópolis, Corrientes, Rosario, Córdoba, Buenos Aires, Salta, and Montevideo test outside. The uneven outline defeats a country-shaped reading.

The target directly shares two arcs with Puri, one with Charrua, and two with Mbyá features. Shared TopoJSON arcs are economical drawing instructions. They do not prove treaties, recognized frontiers, bilingualism, kinship, warfare, or neighborly agreement about whose garden ended beside which stream.

At 1400, tested places carry broad savanna, Tupi, Charrua, or other labels. At 1492 they receive a dense stack of specific and modernized names. At 1500 the exact target vanishes and the owners repaint again. These file seams cannot date origins, borders, migrations, or collective disappearance.

Existing Tupis, Savanna hunter-gatherers, Pampas cultures, Shellfish gatherers, and Aché cards were checked and rejected as substitutes. Each has a different exact association, chronology, polygon, evidence scope, and historical subject. A separate card is necessary even when the imported map makes their colors overlap.

Tekoha joins a physical place with the conditions for living a Guarani way of life: land, forest, fields, water, animals, plants, medicines, homes, gardens, worship, and extended-family relationships. It is lived and made by particular communities. It is not a ready-made state boundary waiting inside a map file.

A Paraguayan Indigenous plan makes the point especially clearly: land is not Guarani tekoha without Guarani people carrying out spiritual and cultural practices there. Territory includes material and immaterial relations. That definition makes the atlas error obvious, because geometry alone cannot manufacture community presence or belonging.

Ñandeva, Kaiowa, and Mbyá communities differ in speech, custom, ritual practice, political and social organization, religion, and responses to history. Relatedness matters, but so does difference. “Guarani” is therefore a family of specific histories, not permission to paste one community’s rules across the entire polygon.

Mbyá sources describe networks of kinship and reciprocity connecting many settlements through visiting, ritual, exchange of craft materials, and cultivated plants. Mobility can strengthen territorial life instead of contradicting it. A tekoha is not a tiny fenced dot, yet neither is it the atlas’s continent-sized blob.

Colonial writers helped create a habit of calling many peoples Guarani and describing wide regions as culturally uniform. A modern historical study calls this “guaranization” of the written record. The card resists that old shortcut by naming local evidence and admitting when identity cannot be recovered.

sections.title: Build homes, settlements, and routes locally

items.text: Archaeological settlements in southern Brazil vary by river, coast, lagoon, soil, and access to forest. Regional survey around Laguna dos Patos combines site distribution, internal structure, artifacts, and environment to reconstruct connected places. One village pattern cannot be enlarged until it covers Paraguay, Bolivia, and southeastern Brazil.

São Paulo research links black anthropogenic earth patches with former large-house spaces, while groups of patches can suggest settlements. This is a tested analogy rather than a universal key. Soil chemistry and excavation help locate activity, but a dark stain is not a family photograph or complete house plan.

A Paraguayan architecture study treats houses, collective spaces, forest access, and territorial relationships together. Buildings are not isolated boxes: materials, orientation, work, visiting, and ceremony connect them with a lived place. Modern documentation can guide respectful questions, though it cannot supply an untouched blueprint for every 1492 settlement.

Santa Catarina archaeology places Guarani arrival on that coast around 1000 CE and studies settlements among rivers, dunes, lagoons, and the ocean. Five centuries later, coastal choices still differed from inland Paraná or Chaco settings. “Near water” describes many options, not one address or seasonal schedule.

At the southern edge, scattered finds in Uruguay come from controlled sites, older collections, isolated discoveries, and colonial contexts of unequal quality. Archaeologists must sort those histories before mapping presence. The evidence is interesting precisely because it is incomplete, even if the atlas prefers a confidently colored shape.

sections.title: Grow, gather, fish, hunt, and share food

items.text: Guarani-associated subsistence combined cultivated plants with fishing, hunting, and gathering in regionally different proportions. Archaeological syntheses identify maize, manioc, beans, squash, peanuts, and other foods, but dates and contexts matter. A crop list describes possibilities and evidence, not the same breakfast in every home.

Vessel microremains from Misiones include maize and squash, while phytoliths and starch help connect some pots with food processing. Microscopic traces recover meals that rarely survive whole. They still require contamination controls, provenience, and comparison, because a single stubborn starch grain should not plan an entire menu.

Forest agriculture depended on fertile soil, water, clearings, and access to fishing, hunting, and gathered foods. São Paulo research describes these choices without reducing the economy to farming alone. Gardens and wild resources belonged to connected landscapes, and neither “farmer” nor “forager” works well as a total identity.

A southern-edge residential synthesis reports hunting, fishing, gathering, and crops including maize, tubers, beans, squash, and peanuts. That evidence belongs to particular late precolonial contexts. The polygon’s Bolivian forests, Paraguay basin, Atlantic coast, and southern grasslands each demand their own environmental and archaeological checks.

Fermented drinks could transform crops into food, hospitality, ceremony, and collective labor, while specialized vessel forms helped prepare and serve them. Archaeologists compare pots, residues, and later records cautiously. A large cup may hint at company, but it cannot identify the guest list or settle who washed up.

sections.title: Make pottery, tools, clothing, and knowledge

items.text: The Célia Maria site in São Paulo produced precolonial pottery dated around 450 years before the study’s reference point. Researchers reconstructed vessel shapes and sequences of technical gestures from rim fragments. Those choices show skilled makers; they do not turn every similar vessel into proof of one political territory.

A Taquari Valley collection yielded reconstructions of seventy-two vessels used for cooking, storing, serving, eating, and drinking. Size, rim, surface, fire traces, and residue can suggest functions. Pots had busy careers, but archaeology should not promote them into passports carrying their owners’ language and ancestry.

Painted, corrugated, smoothed, and otherwise finished ceramics vary across regions and sites. IPHAN’s multi-author synthesis treats that variation as a research problem rather than a single unchanging style. Similarity can reflect learning and connection; difference can reflect choice, task, household, generation, available clay, or contact.

X-ray fluorescence tests the elemental composition of pottery rather than trusting color and surface alone. At southern Brazilian Guarani sites, archaeometry can compare clays and production questions with visual typology. Science adds another clue, not a magic scanner that prints the potter’s name, village, and favorite recipe.

Stone tools, wooden implements, baskets, fibers, feathers, and clothing survive unevenly. IPHAN inventories show why archaeologists protect whole contexts: pottery, points, axes, flakes, ornaments, and shaped objects make more sense together. A beautiful isolated artifact loses much of its date, task, and relationship story.

sections.title: See families, women, visiting, and cooperation

items.text: Modern Guarani accounts place extended families at the center of social, economic, and political organization within particular tekoha. That comparison helps ask how houses and gardens connected people. It cannot provide a fixed 1492 household chart, marriage rule, inheritance system, or leadership title for every archaeological settlement.

Mbyá networks link settlements through visits, kinship, ritual, materials, and cultivated plants. Social life therefore crossed any one village without requiring centralized rule. Relatives arriving with news, seed, craft material, or an invitation could make mobility ordinary, though the exact routes and hosts in 1492 remain unnamed.

Pottery making required clay selection, preparation, coiling or shaping, finishing, firing, repair, and knowledge of suitable forms. Later records often associate pottery with women, but archaeological sherds rarely identify a maker’s gender. The card recognizes women’s probable expertise without assigning every pot to an imaginary universal job chart.

Cooking, gardening, fishing, hunting, gathering, carrying water, tending fires, building, childcare, visiting, and ceremony all required coordination. Evidence preserves some durable tools and spaces better than conversations or care. The missing voices matter, because daily cooperation was more than the pile of objects that happened to survive.

Settlement organization can reveal repeated choices about houses, activity areas, paths, and shared space, but it does not record every dispute or joke. Archaeologists compare eleven Taquari-Antas sites through pottery to study regional relationships. Variation is evidence of real communities making decisions, not failure to match one template.

sections.title: Let children learn, teach, play, and remember

items.text: No securely dated classroom, timetable, alphabet lesson, or named teacher survives for the exact polygon in 1492. Children still had to learn language, gardens, water, fire, tools, food, routes, relationships, and stories. Complex material traditions make teaching certain while leaving its daily form locally specific.

Modern Mbyá research shows children learning and also teaching through song and play. That reverses the idea that knowledge moves only from silent child to speaking adult. It is a specific contemporary comparison, not a transcript of 1492 childhood, yet it widens the questions archaeologists should ask.

Mbyá educators in São Paulo center children, memory, oral knowledge, identity, and ancestral wisdom within modern Indigenous education centers. Their work belongs to current communities confronting present institutions. It cannot be back-projected as an ancient school system, but it demonstrates that education is broader than desks and worksheets.

Research with Mbyá participants treats singing, speaking, writing, observation, and participation as parts of wider knowledge production and transmission. Oral knowledge is not a deficient version of a book. The absence of a surviving 1492 text therefore says something about evidence preservation, not intelligence or historical depth.

Children probably practiced carrying, shaping clay, recognizing plants, tending fires, preparing food, and listening for social cues in age-appropriate ways. Exact ages and duties remain unknown. A tiny fingerprint in clay might be suggestive, but it should not be enrolled immediately in an imaginary pottery kindergarten.

sections.title: Treat health, medicine, birth, and care responsibly

items.text: A community-participatory Mbyá study documents exchanges of medicinal plants among seven southern Brazilian territories. Participants connect forest health with food, medicine, education, knowledge, and culture. This is living, community-specific evidence. It should guide respectful questions, not become a prescription list copied backward five centuries.

Gardens, diverse foods, clean water choices, shelter, fire, rest, and social care all affected health before a named treatment began. Archaeology can recover some foods, houses, vessels, and injuries, but rarely the full diagnosis. No exact-period source establishes one Guarani medical system across this polygon.

Pregnancy, birth, infancy, injury, fever, grief, disability, and aging required knowledge and help, even when care left no durable trace. The card acknowledges caregivers without inventing healer titles, dosages, surgery, or universal ritual. Silence in excavated soil is not proof that nobody nursed or comforted anyone.

Current Guarani health research emphasizes that land, forest, mobility, and exchanged plants shape individual and collective well-being. Those relationships are historically dynamic, especially under land loss. Applying a modern practice unchanged to 1492 would flatten both the ancestors and the specialists who maintain knowledge today.

Human remains and funerary vessels can provide evidence about diet, disease, labor, and ritual, but they are also ancestors, not laboratory supplies without communities. Archaeological stewardship requires context and respect. This card avoids sensational burial claims and does not treat one grave as a medical handbook.

sections.title: Follow water, cleaning, waste, and toilets

items.text: Many settlements favored rivers, springs, fertile floodplains, forests, lagoons, or coasts, but water brought different currents, floods, insects, and seasonal changes. Choosing a home required local knowledge of access and risk. The atlas offers no common well, pipe system, water authority, or one rule for safe drinking.

Vessels carried, stored, heated, fermented, served, and shared liquids. Shape and residue can support those functions, yet no pot automatically proves drinking-water treatment. Cleaning clay containers, replacing damaged ones, and protecting food were practical tasks, though the exact household routines usually vanished with the hands that performed them.

Hearths, food debris, broken pottery, dark earth, and activity areas help reconstruct how settlements managed work and discard. Spatial separation may reduce mess and danger, but no reviewed exact-period feature in this packet is securely identified as a sewer, drain, bathhouse, privy, or latrine.

Modern research across sixty-three Guarani villages records substantial variation in water sources, toilets, waste removal, and housing. It is useful for one conclusion only: sanitation is neither timeless nor uniform. Present hardship reflects current infrastructure and inequality, not an ancient cultural preference that can be projected backward.

People in 1492 managed bodily waste and privacy somehow, but the reviewed archaeology does not reveal a universal toilet design. Camp length, soil, water, flooding, settlement density, and custom could all matter. The honest toilet fact is that a confident answer would currently contain more invention than evidence.

Guarani-associated communities built regional settlement networks, cultivated diverse plants, fished and hunted, navigated major rivers, made technically varied pottery, maintained houses and gardens, exchanged materials, and taught new generations. These achievements were repeated local work. They do not require one capital, ruler, army, or giant polygon to be impressive.

Archaeologists improve the picture by combining survey, stratigraphy, radiocarbon dates, vessel reconstruction, microscopic residues, soil study, environmental evidence, and community knowledge. Each method answers different questions. Agreement among several lines is stronger than a familiar label, while disagreement is a reason to investigate rather than smooth away difference.

No securely localized Guarani writing from 1492 to 1500 was found. Paraguay’s cultural ministry dates Montoya’s published dictionary to 1639 and grammar and bilingual catechism to 1640. Those colonial works are later and mediated, so borrowing even a charming phrase would give this exact-period card a false documentary voice.

Modern written standards also cannot stand for every Guarani community or the late fifteenth century. Paraguay’s language academy governs today’s official Guarani orthography, while Mbyá, Kaiowa, Ñandeva, and other varieties have their own histories. Written sample: none supplied, because precision is more respectful than decorative time travel.

Living practices such as tereré with pohã ñana transmit Guarani words, medicinal-plant knowledge, hospitality, and social memory in Paraguay today. UNESCO’s recognition belongs to a particular living tradition, not a fossil from 1492. Continuity means communities keep creating and teaching, not that culture stayed frozen for centuries.

ending.text: The exact feature ends because the atlas changes categories in 1500, not because a Guarani state collapsed or every tekoha emptied. Representative owners repaint in the software and remain stable at 1530, while communities, families, languages, gardens, travel, worship, and political life continued through their own local histories. European invasion soon brought violence, disease, enslavement, missions, and land loss unevenly across the region, but it did not turn Guarani peoples into one passive population or erase their agency. Mbyá, Kaiowa or Paĩ Tavyterã, Ñandeva or Avá Guarani, and other communities remain distinct living peoples. UNESCO’s work with Guarani communities documenting Arete Guasu in their own language shows continuity as renewal, memory, ancestry, and present action. The map endpoint therefore receives no fall date, conqueror, or successor state. It closes only an erroneous eight-year feature while Guarani histories continue beyond it.
